A second opinion for a mixed model

Source: vignettes/koine.Rmd
koine.Rmd
library(koine)

Why

An analyst has just fitted a mixed model – a random intercept for the blocks in a trial, or two crossed intercepts for variety and trial in a multi-environment trial (MET) – and wants an independent second opinion: not another run of the same sampler on the same posterior, but an opinion built from inference methods and model-structure variants that are genuinely different from whatever produced the first fit. Does a heavy-tailed alternative agree with a Gaussian fit? Does a closed-form treatment of the random effects agree with what a sampler-based fit reported? koine answers by stacking over a curated battery of inference lenses in predictive space and returning one synthesised opinion, or by abstaining outright – declining to guess – when the battery cannot offer enough independent perspectives to say anything. This vignette walks the full spine an analyst would use to get that opinion: the request, the battery that resolves against it, a single lens, the diversity that makes a synthesis worth having, and the two mixed-model shapes koine supports – a single random intercept and a multi-environment trial’s two crossed intercepts – ending with what koine does when it should not answer at all.

What

A koine_pass() is an engine-neutral, declarative request: it carries the formula, the data, an evaluable family, the canonical observation axis, and a content hash, and it is the one object every lens and every synthesis call reads. resolve_battery() enrols only the lenses whose family, feature support and tier fit that request, and records why every other lens was excluded, so absence is always explained rather than silent. A lens’s own fit_*() function – fit_dram(), fit_robust_t(), fit_glmm_marginal(), and others in the registry – takes a pass and returns draws, or a typed abstention if the lens cannot field the model. synthesise() is the front door: it resolves the battery, fits every opinion lens, gates on PSIS reliability, and stacks the survivors into one predictive opinion, reporting the stacking weights, the effective number of distinct components, and an over-dispersed envelope that reflects between-lens disagreement as well as within-lens uncertainty. abstention() and is_abstention() make a decline a typed, first-class value rather than an error or a silently wrong number.

Do

The request: a pass 

set.seed(42)
n_pop <- 40L
x_pop <- rnorm(n_pop)
d_pop <- data.frame(
  y = 1.5 + 0.8 * x_pop + rnorm(n_pop, sd = 0.7), x = x_pop
)
pass <- koine_pass(y ~ x, data = d_pop, family = gaussian())
pass
#> <koine pass>
#>   formula : y ~ x
#>   family  : gaussian / identity
#>   N       : 40
#>   outputs : posterior, log_likelihood
#>   ir_hash : c708f46cca12...

The family is wrapped into an evaluable family_spec: koine computes the pointwise log-likelihood itself, because the upstream family object exposes a mean function but no log-likelihood.

fs <- as_family_spec(gaussian())
fs$loglik_pointwise(y = c(0, 1), eta = c(0, 1), aux = list(sigma = 1))
#> [1] -0.9189385 -0.9189385

The battery 

resolved <- resolve_battery(pass)
vapply(resolved$enrolled, function(lens) lens$id, character(1))
#> [1] "dram"         "nimble_gibbs" "dream_zs"     "robust_t"     "horseshoe"   
#> [6] "lasso"        "ridge"
Lenses excluded from this Gaussian population battery.
Lens Reason excluded
pg_gibbs family ‘gaussian’ unsupported by lens
glmm_marginal feature_unsupported: lens requires a random-effects term
nimble_glmm feature_unsupported: lens requires a random-effects term
robust_re_t3 feature_unsupported: lens requires a random-effects term
robust_re_t8 feature_unsupported: lens requires a random-effects term

Seven lenses resolve for this Gaussian population model: DRAM, NIMBLE-Gibbs and DREAM (different inference families on the same posterior), plus the model-structure variants – robust-t and a shrinkage spectrum (ridge, lasso, horseshoe). The table shows why every other registered lens was left out; the Polya-Gamma Gibbs lens, for instance, is excluded on family grounds because it serves binomial logistic models, not Gaussian ones, while the random-effects lenses are excluded because this particular pass has no grouping term for them to honour.

One lens: delayed-rejection adaptive Metropolis 

fit_pop <- fit_dram(pass, n_iter = 1500L, n_burn = 750L, n_chains = 2L)
fit_pop
#> <koine fb_fit>
#>   status   : contributed
#>   method   : dram  exactness: exact
#>   family/kernel: random_walk / dram
#>   draws    : 750 x 2 x 3 (chain x draw x var)
#>   log_lik  : NULL (unassembled)
#>   maturity : koine-implemented-validated
DRAM posterior summary for the population regression.

b_x 0.792 0.086

Diversity: a heavy-tailed structure variant

koine’s value as a second opinion comes from diversity. Lenses that fit the same model structure only corroborate one another – a useful consistency check, but the stacking weights then collapse onto a single component. Genuine diversity needs a different model structure. The robust-t lens supplies one: a Student-t likelihood whose heavy tails give a materially different predictive when the data depart from Gaussianity. The battery below is restricted to two lenses – DRAM and robust-t – on a synthetic, moderately heavy-tailed toy, so the comparison is exactly this one contrast rather than the full seven-lens battery above.

Engines available on this build

Two later sections need an optional package each: the two figures below need ggplot2, and the MET corroboration check needs lme4. Each guarded chunk checks for its own package and prints one sentence in its place when the package is absent, so the vignette still renders, with less to read, on a build that carries neither.

has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_lme4 <- requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)
set.seed(19)
n_ht <- 60L
x_ht <- rnorm(n_ht)
y_ht <- 1 + 0.8 * x_ht + rt(n_ht, df = 5) * 0.6      # moderately heavy-tailed
pass_ht <- koine_pass(y_ht ~ x_ht, data.frame(y_ht = y_ht, x_ht = x_ht),
                      gaussian())

reg <- koine_stage1_registry()
lens_id <- function(id) which(vapply(reg, function(z) z$id, "") == id)
reg_ht <- list(reg[[lens_id("dram")]], reg[[lens_id("robust_t")]])
reg_ht[[1]]$fit_fn <- function(p, ls) fit_dram(p, ls, 1500L, 750L, 2L)
reg_ht[[2]]$fit_fn <- function(p, ls) {
  fit_robust_t(p, ls, nu = 4, n_iter = 1500L, n_burn = 750L, n_chains = 2L)
}
res_ht <- synthesise(pass_ht, registry = reg_ht)
res_ht
#> <koine result --- synthesised fourth opinion>
#>   components: 2
#>   weights   :
#>     dram           0.449
#>     robust_t       0.551
#>   elpd (stacked LOO): -65.83
#>   PSIS k threshold  : 0.685
#>   diversity         : 1.98 effective lens(es)
#>   pool envelope     : 2 lenses, 0 disagreeing on >=1 obs (95%, 2x inflated)
#>   evidence axis     : 1 lens(es), log-ml [prior-conditional]
Independence declaration for the two-lens heavy-tailed battery.
Lens Sampler family Kernel
dram random_walk dram
robust_t random_walk robust-t-dram

Figure: the stacking weights 

weight_df <- data.frame(
  lens = names(w_ht), weight = as.numeric(w_ht), stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ggplot2::ggplot(
  weight_df, ggplot2::aes(x = stats::reorder(lens, weight), y = weight,
                          fill = lens)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_col() +
  ggplot2::coord_flip() +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "lens", y = "stacking weight",
    title = sprintf("n_eff = %.2f effective lens(es)", n_eff_ht)
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

Stacking weights for the two-lens heavy-tailed battery, with the effective-component count n_eff annotated. Neither lens is at zero, so the mixture is a genuine blend, not a corroboration collapse onto one structure.

Figure: the pooled predictive envelope 

ord_ht <- order(x_ht)
points_df <- data.frame(x = x_ht[ord_ht], y = y_ht[ord_ht])
band_df <- data.frame(
  x = x_ht[ord_ht], lower = lpe_ht$lower[ord_ht], upper = lpe_ht$upper[ord_ht],
  pool_mean = lpe_ht$pool_mean[ord_ht]
)
ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    data = band_df, ggplot2::aes(x = x, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = band_df, ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = pool_mean), colour = "#0072B2",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = points_df, ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y), colour = "grey35", size = 1.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "x", y = "y",
    title = "Pool envelope: pooled mean response and its 95% band"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

The over-dispersed linear-pool envelope for the heavy-tailed battery: the pooled posterior-mean response (line) and its 95% envelope (band), built from the two lenses’ means and their between-lens disagreement, against the fitted x range.

Mixed models: a random intercept

koine also handles a single random intercept, (1 | g). The opinion is built on an axis orthogonal to the sealed engines: NIMBLE-Gibbs (fit_nimble_glmm()) samples the random effects, while the marginal lens (fit_glmm_marginal(), shown here because it needs no extra toolchain) integrates them out – exactly for the Gaussian LMM, by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature for the binomial GLMM. Both report (beta, sigma, tau) and are stacked on the same per-observation integrated predictive (the random effect marginalised under each draw’s variance components), which keeps the leave-one-out gate reliable. (Poisson is enrolled alongside Gaussian and binomial, on a funnel-safe blocked-slice kernel; a post-fit convergence gate makes the lens abstain rather than contribute where the variance component is too weakly identified to mix.)

set.seed(20)
n_re <- 60L
n_groups_re <- 10L
g_re <- factor(rep(seq_len(n_groups_re), each = n_re / n_groups_re))
x_re <- rnorm(n_re)
b_re <- rnorm(n_groups_re, 0, 1.1)                  # group random intercepts
y_re <- 1 + 0.5 * x_re + b_re[g_re] + rnorm(n_re, 0, 0.7)
pass_re <- koine_pass(
  y_re ~ x_re + (1 | g_re), data.frame(y_re = y_re, x_re = x_re, g_re = g_re),
  gaussian()
)
fit_re <- fit_glmm_marginal(pass_re, n_iter = 1500L, n_burn = 750L,
                            n_chains = 2L)
Random-intercept marginal-lens posterior means (b0, sigma, tau).
variable mean
b_(Intercept) 0.896
b_x_re 0.611
sigma 0.687
tau 1.336

A third lens, fit_glmm_robust_re(), gives the random intercepts heavy (Student-t) tails. Where the two Gaussian-RE lenses corroborate (their weights collapse), this structure variant earns real stacking weight when group effects are outlying – so koine’s mixed-model opinion, like its population battery, becomes sensitive to model structure rather than a weighted echo of one assumption.

Multi-environment trials: variety and trial together

The breeder-standard multi-environment-trial (MET) model carries two random intercepts – a variety effect and a trial (environment) effect, crossed (each variety grown across many trials) or nested. koine fits this structure directly with (1 | variety) + (1 | trial), so it corroborates a production MET model on the model that model actually fits, not on a single-random-effect reduction that discards the trial structure. The Gaussian MET marginal stays exact: the random effects are integrated out analytically, through a dense Cholesky of the marginal covariance

V=σ2I+τvariety2ZvarietyZvariety⊤+τtrial2ZtrialZtrial⊤,V = \sigma^2 I + \tau_{\text{variety}}^2 Z_{\text{variety}} Z_{\text{variety}}^\top + \tau_{\text{trial}}^2 Z_{\text{trial}} Z_{\text{trial}}^\top,

where ZvarietyZ_{\text{variety}} and ZtrialZ_{\text{trial}} are the (0/1) grouping indicator matrices for each random factor and τvariety\tau_{\text{variety}}, τtrial\tau_{\text{trial}} are their variance-component standard deviations – where the sealed engines instead sample (NIMBLE) or Laplace-approximate (INLA) them. This is the one fitted example in this vignette that needs two grouping factors rather than one: demonstrating that koine fits a crossed structure at all is the entire point of the section, so the two groupings stay, with every other dimension of the design shrunk instead.

set.seed(404)
n_variety <- 10L                                    # varieties
n_trial <- 5L                                       # trials (environments)
u_variety <- rnorm(n_variety, 0, 1.0)                # variety effects
v_trial <- rnorm(n_trial, 0, 2.5)                    # trial effects (dominant)
rows_met <- vector("list", n_variety)
for (i in seq_len(n_variety)) {
  trials_i <- sample(seq_len(n_trial), 3L)          # incomplete, unbalanced
  obs_i <- lapply(trials_i, function(t) {
    data.frame(
      variety = i, trial = t,
      yield = 5 + u_variety[i] + v_trial[t] + rnorm(1L, 0, 0.6)
    )
  })
  rows_met[[i]] <- do.call(rbind, obs_i)
} # ends i, over the varieties
met <- do.call(rbind, rows_met)
met$variety <- factor(met$variety)
met$trial <- factor(met$trial)
nrow(met)
#> [1] 30

pass_met <- koine_pass(
  yield ~ 1 + (1 | variety) + (1 | trial), met, gaussian(), seed = 5L
)
pass_met                                            # tagged [MET], crossed
#> <koine pass>
#>   formula : yield ~ 1 + (1 | variety) + (1 | trial)
#>   random  : (1 | variety) + (1 | trial)  [MET]
#>   family  : gaussian / identity
#>   N       : 30
#>   outputs : posterior, log_likelihood
#>   ir_hash : b84c3ccf9161...
fit_met <- fit_glmm_marginal(pass_met, n_iter = 1200L, n_burn = 600L,
                             n_chains = 2L)
MET marginal-lens posterior means (b0, sigma, tau_variety, tau_trial).
variable mean
b_(Intercept) 3.484
sigma 0.373
tau_variety 1.185
tau_trial 1.798

The draws carry one tau_<grouping> per random factor. The chunk below checks koine’s MET variety effects against a production MET model (here lme4, fitted by REML), and against a single-random-intercept reduction that confounds each variety with the trials it happened to be grown in.

prod_fit <- lme4::lmer(
  yield ~ 1 + (1 | variety) + (1 | trial), met, REML = TRUE
)
blup_prod <- lme4::ranef(prod_fit)$variety[, 1]
single_fit <- lme4::lmer(yield ~ 1 + (1 | variety), met, REML = TRUE)
blup_single <- lme4::ranef(single_fit)$variety[, 1]

# koine MET variety effects (GLS BLUP at the posterior-mean variance components)
mv_met <- stats::setNames(sm_met$mean, sm_met$variable)
design_met <- koine:::.pass_design(pass_met)
red_met <- koine:::.pass_re_design(pass_met)
taus_met <- c(mv_met["tau_variety"], mv_met["tau_trial"])
vmat_met <- koine:::.re_marginal_cov(
  design_met$N, red_met$factors, taus_met, mv_met["sigma"]
)
b_names <- paste0("b_", colnames(design_met$X))
resid_met <- design_met$y - as.numeric(design_met$X %*% mv_met[b_names])
z_variety <- koine:::.re_indicator(
  red_met$factors[[1L]]$group, red_met$factors[[1L]]$n_groups
)
u_koine <- as.numeric(
  taus_met[1L]^2 * t(z_variety) %*% solve(vmat_met, resid_met)
)

cor_met <- cor(u_koine, blup_prod)
cor_single <- cor(blup_single, blup_prod)
Variety-effect correlation against the production (lme4) MET fit.
comparison correlation
koine MET vs production MET 1.000
single-RE vs production MET 0.928

A non-Gaussian MET – whose dense crossed marginal has no exact quadrature – is declined outright rather than approximated:

counts_met <- transform(met, n = rpois(nrow(met), 4))
fit_glmm_marginal(
  koine_pass(n ~ 1 + (1 | variety) + (1 | trial), counts_met, poisson())
)$reason
#> [1] "feature_unsupported"

Richer structure is refused rather than fitted as the wrong model: a random slope, or more than two grouping factors, makes koine abstain feature_unsupported.

pass_bad <- koine_pass(
  y_re ~ x_re + (x_re | g_re),
  data.frame(y_re = y_re, x_re = x_re, g_re = g_re), gaussian()
)
synthesise(pass_bad)$reason
#> [1] "feature_unsupported"

When koine abstains

Abstention is a first-class outcome, not an error. If fewer than two independent opinion lenses resolve – for instance with a single-lens battery – koine declines to guess and says why.

out_abstain <- synthesise(pass, registry = list(koine_stage1_registry()[[1]]))
is_abstention(out_abstain)
#> [1] TRUE
out_abstain
#> <koine abstention>
#>   scope : synthesis
#>   reason: no_diverse_battery
#>   detail: only 1 opinion lens(es) resolved; >= 2 independent lenses needed.

Read

The DRAM lens recovers the data-generating intercept and slope closely: 1.57 against a true 1.5, and 0.79 against a true 0.8.

On the heavy-tailed toy, the two-lens battery does not collapse onto a single structure: DRAM carries 0.45 of the stacking weight and robust-t carries 0.55, giving 1.98 effective lens(es) – above the package’s degeneracy threshold of 1.5, so the diagnostic records genuine diversity rather than a corroboration collapse. The weights figure shows that split directly, and the envelope figure shows what it buys: a pooled band wide enough that, on this particular draw, 0 of the 60 points fall outside the 95% band even though the band is inflated for between-lens disagreement as well as within-lens uncertainty.

The single-random-intercept marginal lens recovers the data-generating values in the same qualitative way: intercept 0.9 (true 1), slope 0.61 (true 0.5), residual SD 0.69 (true 0.7) and group SD 1.34 (true 1.1), on 60 observations in 10 groups – fewer groups than a production analysis would carry, which is why the variance component is recovered only qualitatively rather than to two decimal places.

On the multi-environment toy, koine’s MET marginal variety effects correlate 1.0000 with the production (lme4) MET fit, against 0.9280 for the single-random-intercept reduction that ignores the trial structure. The gap between the two reproduces, at this much smaller scale, the qualitative point the section makes: confounding a variety with the trials it happened to be grown in costs real agreement with the model that actually generated the data, even on an incomplete, unbalanced design of only 30 records.

Every abstention in this vignette is grounded in the same registry the battery table used above: the Poisson MET call, the random-slope call, and the single-lens synthesise() call all decline through the typed koine_abstention path (is_abstention() returns TRUE for the last of the three) rather than returning a silently wrong number.

Limits

The random-effects lenses carry a fixed weakly-informative prior – N(0, 5) on every fixed-effect coefficient and lognormal(0, 2) on every variance-component standard deviation for the Gaussian and binomial families – and koine_pass()’s prior argument, though present in the signature, does not reach them: it is reserved for lenses that do not yet exist. On a response measured in the tens or hundreds this reference prior pulls the intercept toward zero and lets the group standard deviation absorb the resulting offset, because the prior’s own scale, not the data’s, starts to dominate the posterior. The examples in this vignette are engineered on roughly unit scale for exactly this reason: they are not a demonstration that the prior is harmless, only that it is invisible when the design already matches its assumption. A caller with a response in its raw, natural units – yield in kilograms per hectare, a count in the hundreds, anything not already standardised – should centre and scale the response and every non-intercept covariate before building the pass, and map any recovered coefficients back to the original scale afterwards; the random-intercept and MET marginal lenses in this vignette would return a materially different, prior-dominated opinion on the same data left in its natural units.

Every fitted example in this vignette uses at most 60 observations and a few hundred to two thousand MCMC iterations over two chains, chosen so the whole vignette renders in under two minutes rather than to reflect the scale koine is meant to run at; the MET section is the one exception, because demonstrating a crossed two-grouping structure at all needs two grouping factors, so it shrinks every other dimension of the design instead. The two-lens diversity split shown above is itself sensitive to this small a sample: at n = 60, most seeds tried while preparing this vignette gave a degenerate, single-lens-dominated split rather than the genuine two-lens blend shown here, whereas the same scenario at a few hundred observations is far less seed-sensitive. A reader who wants a diversity diagnostic that does not depend on which random draw they happened to get should run the same battery at production scale, not at this vignette’s render-time scale.

The MET marginal is exact only for the Gaussian identity-link case; a non-Gaussian MET routes through a marginalised sampler that can itself abstain on convergence grounds, and that sampler is not exercised in this vignette (the Poisson MET example above abstains before any sampling is attempted, because the structure itself, not a convergence failure, is what is declined). koine’s random-effects corner is limited throughout to a single random intercept or the two-grouping MET structure: random slopes, correlated random effects, and more than two crossed or nested groupings are all refused rather than approximated, as the random-slope example above shows.

What to read next

The package’s own INTEGRATION.md (installed alongside the package, system.file("INTEGRATION.md", package = "koine")) specifies the contract a parent triangulation package drives to use koine as a fourth, synthesised witness, including the exact supported-model corner this vignette exercises. The quorum package’s Getting started with quorum vignette shows koine consumed as one lens in a wider quorum of independent estimates, through its emit_koine() wrapper; that wrapper standardises the response and covariates before calling koine, which is the practical answer to the prior-scale limit stated above.

Reproduce

Seeds are set per section (42 for the population regression, 19 for the heavy-tailed diversity toy, 20 for the random-intercept toy, 404 for the MET toy) so each fitted example is reproducible on its own; package versions follow.
